reviews.question: An inventor claims a thermal engine operates between ocean layers at 27°C and 10°C. It produces 10 kW and discharges 9900 kJ/min. Such an engine is
reviews.explanation:
T₁ = 27°C ≈ 300 K and T₂ = 10°C ≈ 283 K.
The maximum (Carnot) efficiency is ηₘₐₓ = 1 − T₂/T₁ = 1 − 283/300 = 0.05667 = 5.667%.
The heat rejection rate is 9900/60 = 165 kW. Energy balance gives Q̇ₛ = Ẇ + Q̇ᵣₑⱼ = 10 + 165 = 175 kW.
The claimed actual efficiency is ηₐ = Ẇ/Q̇ₛ = 10/175 = 0.05714 = 5.714%.
Because ηₐ > ηₘₐₓ, the claim violates the second law and the engine is impossible. The exact kelvin conversion gives ηₘₐₓ = 17/300.15 ≈ 5.664%, with the same conclusion.

reviews.question: The efficiency of Carnot cycle is maximum for
reviews.explanation: Between specified source and sink temperatures, a reversible engine has the maximum thermal efficiency: ηᵣₑᵥ > ηᵢᵣᵣₑᵥ. A Carnot cycle consists entirely of reversible processes and satisfies ∮δQᵣₑᵥ/T = 0. Thus the intended choice is the reversible engine.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
In a reversible engine the efficiency of the Carnot cycle is maximum.
ηᵣₑᵥₑᵣₛᵢᵦₗₑ > ηᵢᵣᵣₑᵥₑᵣₛᵢᵦₗₑ.
Each process is reversible: ∮(dQ/T) = 0.
reviews.note: The comparison is for engines operating between the same two thermal reservoirs; that necessary condition is explicit in the checked explanation.

reviews.question: According to Kelvin-Planck's statement of second law of thermodynamics.

options.a: It is impossible to construct an engine working on a cyclic process, whose sole purpose is to convert heat energy into work.
options.b: It is possible to construct an engine working on a cyclic process, whose on a cyclic process, whose sole purpose is to convert heat energy into work.
options.c: It is impossible to construct a device which operates in a cyclic process and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a cold body to a hot body.

reviews.explanation:
Kelvin–Planck statement: a cyclic heat engine cannot produce net work while exchanging heat only with a single fixed-temperature reservoir. It cannot have complete conversion of the absorbed heat into work as its sole effect. This is choice (a).
Clausius statement: a cyclic device cannot have as its sole effect the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body. Choice (c) states this equivalent formulation.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Second Law of Thermodynamics:
• Kelvin–Planck statement: It is impossible for a heat engine to produce net work in a complete cycle if it exchanges heat only with bodies at a single fixed temperature.
• Clausius statement: It is impossible to construct a device which, operating in a cycle, will produce no effect other than the transfer of heat from a cooler body to a hotter body.

reviews.question: A Carnot cycle operates between two temperatures T₁ and T₂ (T₁ > T₂). If T₁ is increased by ΔT and T₂ is decreased by ΔT, the efficiency η₂ in the second case and the efficiency η₁ in the first case are related by:
reviews.explanation:
The initial Carnot efficiency is η₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁.
After raising the source temperature and lowering the sink temperature by ΔT > 0, η₂ = 1 − (T₂ − ΔT)/(T₁ + ΔT).
η₂ − η₁ = ΔT(T₁ + T₂)/[T₁(T₁ + ΔT)] > 0 for physical positive temperatures. Therefore η₂ > η₁.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Efficiency of Carnot cycle: η₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁.
η₂ = 1 − (T₂ − ΔT)/(T₁ + ΔT).
As T₂ decreases and T₁ increases, η increases.
η₂ > η₁.

reviews.question: Which law of thermodynamics can be termed as law of degradation of energy?
reviews.explanation: The second law of thermodynamics is termed the law of degradation of energy: although the first law conserves total energy, irreversibility reduces its ability to produce useful work. A cyclic heat engine receiving heat from a source cannot convert it all into work; some heat must be rejected to a sink. Thus the intended choice is the second law.
reviews.sourceExplanation: The second law of thermodynamics is termed the law of degradation of energy. This law states that if energy is transferred to the system then the whole energy cannot be converted to work; some energy will move into the sink.

reviews.question: The efficiency of Carnot engine is 25%. The efficiency is increased to 30% when the sink temperature is reduced by 20°C . What will be the source temperature?
reviews.explanation:
Let T₁ be the fixed absolute source temperature and T₂ the initial sink temperature.
Initially, 0.25 = 1 − T₂/T₁. After lowering the sink by 20°C (a 20 K interval), 0.30 = 1 − (T₂ − 20)/T₁.
Subtracting the initial equation from the final equation gives −(T₂ − 20)/T₁ + T₂/T₁ = 0.05.
Thus (−T₂ + 20 + T₂)/T₁ = 0.05, so 20/T₁ = 0.05.
T₁ = 20/0.05 = 2000/5 = 400 K.

Let T₁ be the fixed absolute source temperature and T₂ the initial sink temperature.

reviews.question: A heat engine is supplied with 1200 kW of heat at a constant temperature of 600 K and it rejects 700 kW of heat at 300 K. Which of the following is true for this heat engine?

options.d: The efficiency of this cycle is greater than 50%

reviews.explanation:
Given Q̇ₛ = 1200 kW at Tₕ = 600 K and Q̇ᵣ = 700 kW at Tₗ = 300 K.
The actual thermal efficiency is η₁ = (Q̇ₛ − Q̇ᵣ)/Q̇ₛ = (500/1200) × 100% = 41.67%.
The reversible limit is η₂ = (1 − Tₗ/Tₕ) × 100% = (1 − 300/600) × 100% = 50%.
The actual efficiency is below the reversible limit. Equivalently, the total reservoir entropy generation rate is 700/300 − 1200/600 = 1/3 kW/K > 0. The cycle is possible and irreversible.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Heat supplied Qₛ = 1200 kW; Tₕ = 600 K.
Heat rejected Qᵣ = 700 kW; Tₗ = 300 K.
η₁ = [(Qₛ − Qᵣ)/Qₛ] × 100 = (500/1200) × 100 = 41.66%.
η₂ = (1 − Tₗ/Tₕ) × 100 = (1 − 300/600) × 100 = (1/2) × 100 = 50%.
η₁ ≠ η₂; therefore it is an irreversible cycle.
reviews.note: Question, options, printed key and complete adjacent explanation checked against the scan; result independently checked using the cited thermodynamic relations.

reviews.question: A reversible heat engine is operating between 800°C and 30°C. The least rate of heat rejection per kW of net output of the engine is:
reviews.explanation:
T₁ = 800°C ≈ 1073 K, T₂ = 30°C ≈ 303 K, and Ẇₙₑₜ = 1 kW.
The reversible engine has the maximum efficiency and hence the least required heat input and heat rejection for this output:

Q̇₂ = Q̇₁ − Ẇₙₑₜ = 1.392 − 1 = 0.392 kW ≈ 0.4 kW. This is the least rate of heat rejection.

reviews.question: In the figure shown below, E is the heat engine with efficiency 0.4 and R is the refrigerator. If Q₂ + Q₄ = 3Q₁, the COP of the refrigerator will be:
reviews.explanation:
Given ηₕₑ = W/Q₁ = 0.4, so W = 0.4Q₁.
For the engine, Q₁ − Q₂ = 0.4Q₁ and therefore Q₂ = 0.6Q₁.
The condition Q₂ + Q₄ = 3Q₁ gives 0.6Q₁ + Q₄ = 3Q₁, so Q₄ = 2.4Q₁.
The refrigerator has Q₃ = Q₄ − W.
COPᵣ = Q₃/W = (Q₄ − W)/W = Q₄/W − 1
       = 2.4Q₁/(0.4Q₁) − 1 = 6 − 1 = 5.

reviews.question: 0.5 kg of air (ideal gas) executes a Carnot power cycle having a thermal efficiency of 50 percent. The heat transfer to the air during the isothermal expansion is 40 kJ. At the beginning of the isothermal expansion the pressure is 7 bar and the volume is 0.12 m’. Determine the maximum and minimum temperature for the cycle in K.
reviews.explanation:
At the start of isothermal expansion, P₁V₁ = mRT₁.
With P₁ = 7 × 10⁵ Pa, V₁ = 0.12 m³, m = 0.5 kg and R = 287 J/(kg·K):
7 × 10⁵ × 0.12 = 0.5 × 287 × T₁.
The maximum temperature is T₁ = 585.4 K.
For the Carnot cycle, η = (T₁ − T₂)/T₁ = 0.5.
Thus 0.5 = (585.4 − T₂)/585.4 and the minimum temperature is T₂ = 292.7 K. The supplied 40 kJ heat input is not required to find these temperatures.

reviews.question: The efficiency of Carnot Cycle may be increased by
reviews.explanation:
For a Carnot cycle between the highest absolute temperature T₁ and lowest absolute temperature T₂, ηc = 1 − T₂/T₁.
At fixed T₂, increasing T₁ lowers T₂/T₁ and increases efficiency; this is option (a). At fixed T₁, decreasing T₂ also lowers T₂/T₁ and increases efficiency; this is option (d). Options (b) and (c) decrease efficiency.
Both (a) and (d) are correct, exactly as the source marker “(a & d)” states. No unique single option can be graded.
The source also explains that practical increases in maximum temperature are limited by metallurgical properties. This is a design limitation, not a change to the Carnot relation: both reservoir temperatures determine the efficiency.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Efficiency of Carnot cycle between two temperature limits T₁ and T₂: ηc = 1 − T₂/T₁.
T₂ is the lowest temperature; T₁ is the highest temperature.
Efficiency may be increased by lowering the lowest temperature and increasing the highest temperature.
The efficiency of the Carnot cycle mainly depends upon the lower temperature, because the highest temperature depends upon metallurgical properties, so we cannot increase it beyond a limit.
reviews.note: Explicit multiple-answer marker (a & d) retained literally. Both alternatives independently verified; grading disabled.

reviews.question: If the COP of a Carnot refrigerator is 6, then the ratio of higher temperature to lower is :
reviews.explanation:

Tₕ/Tₗ = 1/6 + 1 = 7/6. The ratio is 7:6.

reviews.question: A thermal reservoir is a body of
reviews.explanation:
An ideal thermal reservoir has infinite heat capacity and can supply or absorb heat without changing its temperature. Real large bodies approximate this behavior over a finite heat exchange.
The printed examples are the atmosphere, an ocean, a river, an industrial furnace and a two-phase liquid–vapour mixture. A two-phase mixture can remain at its saturation temperature while its phase fractions change.
A reservoir that supplies heat is a source; a reservoir that absorbs heat is a sink.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
A thermal reservoir is a large body with infinite heat capacity which can supply or absorb unlimited quantities of heat without appreciable change in its temperature.
Examples: atmosphere, ocean, river, industrial furnace, two-phase mixture of liquid and vapour.
• If it supplies heat, it is called a source.
• If it absorbs heat, it is called a sink.

reviews.question: A heat engine using lake water at 12 °C as source and the surrounding atmosphere at 2°C as sink executes 1080 cycles per min. If the amount of heat drawn a per cycle is 57 J, then the output of the engine will be :
reviews.explanation:
The rate of heat input is Q̇₁ = 57 × 1080 J/min = 61560 J/min = 1026 W.
For a reversible engine between 12°C ≈ 285 K and 2°C ≈ 275 K, ηₘₐₓ = 1 − 275/285 ≈ 0.03509. The maximum output is Ẇₘₐₓ = ηₘₐₓQ̇₁ ≈ 36 W.
The printed solution uses η ≈ 0.035 and obtains Ẇ = 0.035 × 1026 ≈ 36 W, option (d). However, the question does not say Carnot, reversible or maximum output; an arbitrary engine can have a lower efficiency. The actual output is therefore not uniquely specified.
reviews.note: Printed choice (d) is the Carnot maximum, requiring an unstated reversible/maximum assumption; actual output cannot be uniquely graded.

reviews.question: In a Carnot cycle operating between 200°C and —20°C. If the system receives 90 kJ from the source then the net work done is :
reviews.explanation:
Tₕ = 200°C ≈ 473 K, Tₗ = −20°C ≈ 253 K and Qₛ = 90 kJ.
For a Carnot cycle, η = Wₙₑₜ/Qₛ = (Tₕ − Tₗ)/Tₕ.
Wₙₑₜ/90 = (473 − 253)/473, so Wₙₑₜ = (220/473) × 90 ≈ 41.86 kJ.
Using exact kelvin temperatures gives 90 × 220/473.15 ≈ 41.85 kJ. None of the printed alternatives matches this result. The printed key (c), 42.84 kJ, is inconsistent with both the data and the source derivation.

reviews.question: A heat engine receives 1 kW of heat transfer at 1200 K and gives out 600 W as work, with the rest as heat transfer to the ambient at 300 K. The second law efficiency of the engine is :
reviews.explanation:
Heat supplied Q̇ₛ = 1 kW = 1000 W and Ẇₙₑₜ = 600 W. Tₕ = 1200 K and Tₗ = 300 K.

The maximum efficiency is ηₘₐₓ = (Tₕ − Tₗ)/Tₕ = 1 − Tₗ/Tₕ = 1 − 300/1200 = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
The second-law efficiency is ηⅡ = ηₐ/ηₘₐₓ = (0.60/0.75) × 100% = 80%.

reviews.question: A heat engine receives half of its heat supply at 1000 K and remaining half at 500 K. Heat is rejected to the sink at 300 K. The maximum thermal efficiency of the heat engine will be:
reviews.explanation:
Let the total heat supply be Q, so Q₁ = Q₂ = Q/2. The maximum efficiency occurs for a reversible engine.
Its entropy balance is Q/2000 + Q/1000 − Qᵣ/300 = 0.
Thus 3Q/2000 = Qᵣ/300, giving Qᵣ/Q = 9/20.
ηₘₐₓ = 1 − Qᵣ/(Q/2 + Q/2) = 1 − Qᵣ/Q = 1 − 9/20 = 55%.

reviews.question: Consider the following statements: 1. The entropy ofa pure crystalline substance at absolute zero temperature is zero. 2. The efficiency of a reversible heat engine is independent of the nature of the working substance and depends only on_ the temperature of the reservoirs between which it operates. 3. Carnot’s theorem states that of all heat engines operating between a given constant temperature source and a given constant temperature sink, none has a_ higher efficiency than a reversible engine. Which of the above statements are correct?
reviews.explanation:
Statement 1 is the third-law result for a pure, perfect crystal with a unique ground state: its entropy at absolute zero is zero.
For a reversible heat engine between two reservoirs, η = 1 − Tₗ/Tₕ. Hence its efficiency depends on reservoir temperatures and not on the working substance, so Statement 2 is correct.
Carnot’s theorem states that no engine operating between a fixed-temperature source and sink can be more efficient than a reversible engine between those same reservoirs, so Statement 3 is correct. Therefore 1, 2 and 3 are correct.
A reversible Carnot cycle is an ideal limit that real engines approach but do not attain; another reversible engine between the same reservoirs has exactly the same efficiency.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
(i) The third law of thermodynamics defines the absolute zero of entropy. The entropy of a pure crystalline substance at absolute zero temperature is zero.
(ii) Efficiency of Carnot = 1 − Tₗ/Tₕ.
It is clear that the efficiency of a Carnot engine depends upon the temperatures of the reservoirs. The working substance does not play any role in its efficiency. Every heat engine works between two temperature limits and gives some work output.
Carnot is an ideal case of engines that is not possible. No heat engine can be as efficient as Carnot.
reviews.note: Answer (d) is correct under the conventional perfect-crystal third-law condition. Corrected the source’s final overstatement: any reversible engine between the same two reservoirs equals Carnot efficiency.

reviews.question: A reversible heat engine receives 2 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 1000 K and a certain amount of heat from a reservoir at 800 K. It rejects 1 kJ of heat to a reservoir at 400 K. The net work output (in kJ) of the cycle is
reviews.explanation:

The first law gives W = (Q₁ + Q₂) − Q₃ = (2 + 0.4) − 1 = 1.4 kJ.

reviews.question: Compute the power required to drive a reversible refrigerator if 100 kJ/min is absorbed from the cold region and the isothermal process occurs at 40°C and -5°C.
reviews.explanation:
Given heat absorbed Q̇ₗ = 100 kJ/min, Tₗ = −5°C ≈ 268 K and Tₕ = 40°C ≈ 313 K.
For the reversible refrigerator, COPᵣ = Tₗ/(Tₕ − Tₗ) = Q̇ₗ/P.
268/(313 − 268) = 100/P.
Thus P = 4500/268 = 16.79 kJ/min ≈ 17 kJ/min. (This is approximately 0.280 kW.)
